title: JS MCQ #1.1: What's the output?
explanation: Within the function, we first declare the `name` variable with the `var` keyword. This means that the variable gets hoisted (memory space is set up during the creation phase) with the default value of `undefined`, until we actually get to the line where we define the variable. We haven't defined the variable yet on the line where we try to log the `name` variable, so it still holds the value of `undefined`. Variables with the `let` keyword (and `const`) are hoisted, but unlike `var`, don't get initialized. They are not accessible before the line we declare (initialize) them. This is called the "temporal dead zone". When we try to access the variables before they are declared, JavaScript throws a `ReferenceError`.
patternExplanation: Tests knowledge of JavaScript scoping, hoisting, and runtime behavior.

title: JS MCQ #1.2: What's the output?
explanation:
Because of the event queue in JavaScript, the `setTimeout` callback function is called _after_ the loop has been executed. Since the variable `i` in the first loop was declared using the `var` keyword, this value was global. During the loop, we incremented the value of `i` by `1` each time, using the unary operator `++`. By the time the `setTimeout` callback function was invoked, `i` was equal to `3` in the first example.

In the second loop, the variable `i` was declared using the `let` keyword: variables declared with the `let` (and `const`) keyword are block-scoped (a block is anything between `{ }`). During each iteration, `i` will have a new value, and each value is scoped inside the loop.
patternExplanation: Tests knowledge of JavaScript scoping, hoisting, and runtime behavior.

title: JS MCQ #1.3: What's the output?
explanation:
Note that the value of `diameter` is a regular function, whereas the value of `perimeter` is an arrow function.

With arrow functions, the `this` keyword refers to its current surrounding scope, unlike regular functions! This means that when we call `perimeter`, it doesn't refer to the shape object, but to its surrounding scope (window for example).

Since there is no value `radius` in the scope of the arrow function, `this.radius` returns `undefined` which, when multiplied by `2 * Math.PI`, results in `NaN`.
patternExplanation: Tests knowledge of JavaScript scoping, hoisting, and runtime behavior.

title: JS MCQ #1.4: What's the output?

patternExplanation: Tests knowledge of JavaScript scoping, hoisting, and runtime behavior.

title: JS MCQ #1.5: Which one is true?
explanation:
In JavaScript, all object keys are strings (unless it's a Symbol). Even though we might not _type_ them as strings, they are always converted into strings under the hood.

JavaScript interprets (or unboxes) statements. When we use bracket notation, it sees the first opening bracket `[` and keeps going until it finds the closing bracket `]`. Only then, it will evaluate the statement.

`mouse[bird.size]`: First it evaluates `bird.size`, which is `"small"`. `mouse["small"]` returns `true`

However, with dot notation, this doesn't happen. `mouse` does not have a key called `bird`, which means that `mouse.bird` is `undefined`. Then, we ask for the `size` using dot notation: `mouse.bird.size`. Since `mouse.bird` is `undefined`, we're actually asking `undefined.size`. This isn't valid, and will throw an error similar to `Cannot read property "size" of undefined`.
patternExplanation: Tests knowledge of JavaScript scoping, hoisting, and runtime behavior.

title: JS MCQ #1.6: What's the output?
explanation: In JavaScript, all objects interact by _reference_ when setting them equal to each other. First, variable `c` holds a value to an object. Later, we assign `d` with the same reference that `c` has to the object. When you change one object, you change all of them.

title: JS MCQ #1.7: What's the output?
explanation:
`new Number()` is a built-in function constructor. Although it looks like a number, it's not really a number: it has a bunch of extra features and is an object.

When we use the `==` operator (Equality operator), it only checks whether it has the same _value_. They both have the value of `3`, so it returns `true`.

However, when we use the `===` operator (Strict equality operator), both value _and_ type should be the same. It's not: `new Number()` is not a number, it's an **object**. Both return `false.`
patternExplanation: Tests knowledge of JavaScript scoping, hoisting, and runtime behavior.

3. `self.greetign` in web workers.
4. `globalThis.greetign` in all environments.

In order to avoid this, we can use `"use strict"`. This makes sure that you have declared a variable before setting it equal to anything.

title: JS MCQ #2.5: All object have prototypes.
description: What is the output?
explanation: All objects have prototypes, except for the **base object**. The base object is the object created by the user, or an object that is created using the `new` keyword. The base object has access to some methods and properties, such as `.toString`. This is the reason why you can use built-in JavaScript methods! All of such methods are available on the prototype. Although JavaScript can't find it directly on your object, it goes down the prototype chain and finds it there, which makes it accessible for you.

title: JS MCQ #2.6: What's the output?
explanation:
JavaScript is a **dynamically typed language**: we don't specify what types certain variables are. Values can automatically be converted into another type without you knowing, which is called _implicit type coercion_. **Coercion** is converting from one type into another.

In this example, JavaScript converts the number `1` into a string, in order for the function to make sense and return a value. During the addition of a numeric type (`1`) and a string type (`'2'`), the number is treated as a string. We can concatenate strings like `"Hello" + "World"`, so what's happening here is `"1" + "2"` which returns `"12"`.

The **prefix** unary operator `++`:

2. Returns the value (this returns `2`)

explanation:
When testing equality, primitives are compared by their _value_, while objects are compared by their _reference_. JavaScript checks if the objects have a reference to the same location in memory.

The two objects that we are comparing don't have that: the object we passed as a parameter refers to a different location in memory than the object we used in order to check equality.

This is why both `{ age: 18 } === { age: 18 }` and `{ age: 18 } == { age: 18 }` return `false`.

title: JS MCQ #3.10: What's the output?
explanation:
Object keys are automatically converted into strings. We are trying to set an object as a key to object `a`, with the value of `123`.

However, when we stringify an object, it becomes `"[object Object]"`. So what we are saying here, is that `a["[object Object]"] = 123`. Then, we can try to do the same again. `c` is another object that we are implicitly stringifying. So then, `a["[object Object]"] = 456`.

Then, we log `a[b]`, which is actually `a["[object Object]"]`. We just set that to `456`, so it returns `456`.

title: JS MCQ #3.11: What's the output?
explanation: We have a `setTimeout` function and invoked it first. Yet, it was logged last. This is because in browsers, we don't just have the runtime engine, we also have something called a `WebAPI`. The `WebAPI` gives us the `setTimeout` function to start with, and for example the DOM. After the _callback_ is pushed to the WebAPI, the `setTimeout` function itself (but not the callback!) is popped off the stack. Now, `foo` gets invoked, and `"First"` is being logged. `foo` is popped off the stack, and `baz` gets invoked. `"Third"` gets logged. The WebAPI can't just add stuff to the stack whenever it's ready. Instead, it pushes the callback function to something called the _queue_. This is where an event loop starts to work. An **event loop** looks at the stack and task queue. If the stack is empty, it takes the first thing on the queue and pushes it onto the stack. `bar` gets invoked, `"Second"` gets logged, and it's popped off the stack.
patternExplanation: Tests knowledge of JavaScript scoping, hoisting, and runtime behavior.

title: JS MCQ #4.9: What's the output?

title: JS MCQ #4.10: Everything in JavaScript is either a...
description: What is the output?
explanation:
JavaScript only has primitive types and objects.

Primitive types are `boolean`, `null`, `undefined`, `bigint`, `number`, `string`, and `symbol`.

What differentiates a primitive from an object is that primitives do not have any properties or methods; however, you'll note that `'foo'.toUpperCase()` evaluates to `'FOO'` and does not result in a `TypeError`. This is because when you try to access a property or method on a primitive like a string, JavaScript will implicitly wrap the primitive type using one of the wrapper classes, i.e. `String`, and then immediately discard the wrapper after the expression evaluates. All primitives except for `null` and `undefined` exhibit this behavior.
patternExplanation: Tests knowledge of JavaScript scoping, hoisting, and runtime behavior.

title: JS MCQ #5.5: What's the output?
explanation:
Regular functions cannot be stopped mid-way after invocation. However, a generator function can be "stopped" midway, and later continue from where it stopped. Every time a generator function encounters a `yield` keyword, the function yields the value specified after it. Note that the generator function in that case doesn’t _return_ the value, it _yields_ the value.

First, we initialize the generator function with `i` equal to `10`. We invoke the generator function using the `next()` method. The first time we invoke the generator function, `i` is equal to `10`. It encounters the first `yield` keyword: it yields the value of `i`. The generator is now "paused", and `10` gets logged.

Then, we invoke the function again with the `next()` method. It starts to continue where it stopped previously, still with `i` equal to `10`. Now, it encounters the next `yield` keyword, and yields `i * 2`. `i` is equal to `10`, so it returns `10 * 2`, which is `20`. This results in `10, 20`.
patternExplanation: Tests knowledge of JavaScript scoping, hoisting, and runtime behavior.

title: JS MCQ #5.6: What does this return?
explanation: When we pass multiple promises to the `Promise.race` method, it resolves/rejects the _first_ promise that resolves/rejects. To the `setTimeout` method, we pass a timer: 500ms for the first promise (`firstPromise`), and 100ms for the second promise (`secondPromise`). This means that the `secondPromise` resolves first with the value of `'two'`. `res` now holds the value of `'two'`, which gets logged.

title: JS MCQ #5.7: What's the output?
explanation: First, we declare a variable `person` with the value of an object that has a `name` property. Then, we declare a variable called `members`. We set the first element of that array equal to the value of the `person` variable. Objects interact by _reference_ when setting them equal to each other. When you assign a reference from one variable to another, you make a _copy_ of that reference. (note that they don't have the _same_ reference!) Then, we set the variable `person` equal to `null`. We are only modifying the value of the `person` variable, and not the first element in the array, since that element has a different (copied) reference to the object. The first element in `members` still holds its reference to the original object. When we log the `members` array, the first element still holds the value of the object, which gets logged.
patternExplanation: Tests knowledge of JavaScript scoping, hoisting, and runtime behavior.

title: JS MCQ #5.8: What's the output?
explanation: With a `for-in` loop, we can iterate through object keys, in this case `name` and `age`. Under the hood, object keys are strings (if they're not a Symbol). On every loop, we set the value of `item` equal to the current key it’s iterating over. First, `item` is equal to `name`, and gets logged. Then, `item` is equal to `age`, which gets logged.

title: JS MCQ #5.9: What's the output?
description:
What is the output?

```javascript
console.log(3 + 4 + '5');
```
explanation:
Operator associativity is the order in which the compiler evaluates the expressions, either left-to-right or right-to-left. This only happens if all operators have the _same_ precedence. We only have one type of operator: `+`. For addition, the associativity is left-to-right.

`3 + 4` gets evaluated first. This results in the number `7`.

`7 + '5'` results in `"75"` because of coercion. JavaScript converts the number `7` into a string, see question 15. We can concatenate two strings using the `+`operator. `"7" + "5"` results in `"75"`.
patternExplanation: Tests knowledge of JavaScript scoping, hoisting, and runtime behavior.

title: JS MCQ #5.10: What's the value of `num`?
description:
What is the output?

```javascript
const num = parseInt('7*6', 10);
```
explanation:
Only the first number in the string is returned. Based on the _radix_ (the second argument in order to specify what type of number we want to parse it to: base 10, hexadecimal, octal, binary, etc.), the `parseInt` checks whether the characters in the string are valid. Once it encounters a character that isn't a valid number in the radix, it stops parsing and ignores the following characters.

`*` is not a valid number. It only parses `"7"` into the decimal `7`. `num` now holds the value of `7`.
patternExplanation: Tests knowledge of JavaScript scoping, hoisting, and runtime behavior.

title: JS MCQ #5.11: What's the output?

In this case, the elements are numbers, so the condition of the if statement `typeof num === "number"` returns `true`. The map function creates a new array and inserts the values returned from the function.

However, we don’t return a value. When we don’t return a value from the function, the function returns `undefined`. For every element in the array, the function block gets called, so for each element we return `undefined`.
patternExplanation: Tests knowledge of JavaScript scoping, hoisting, and runtime behavior.

title: JS MCQ #6.1: What's the output?
explanation:
Arguments are passed by _value_, unless their value is an object, then they're passed by _reference_. `birthYear` is passed by value, since it's a string, not an object. When we pass arguments by value, a _copy_ of that value is created (see question 46).

The variable `birthYear` has a reference to the value `"1997"`. The argument `year` also has a reference to the value `"1997"`, but it's not the same value as `birthYear` has a reference to. When we update the value of `year` by setting `year` equal to `"1998"`, we are only updating the value of `year`. `birthYear` is still equal to `"1997"`.

The value of `person` is an object. The argument `member` has a (copied) reference to the _same_ object. When we modify a property of the object `member` has a reference to, the value of `person` will also be modified, since they both have a reference to the same object. `person`'s `name` property is now equal to the value `"Lydia"`
patternExplanation: Tests knowledge of JavaScript scoping, hoisting, and runtime behavior.

title: JS MCQ #6.2: What's the output?
explanation: With the `throw` statement, we can create custom errors. With this statement, you can throw exceptions. An exception can be a string, a number, a boolean or an object. In this case, our exception is the string `'Hello world!'`. With the `catch` statement, we can specify what to do if an exception is thrown in the `try` block. An exception is thrown: the string `'Hello world!'`. `e` is now equal to that string, which we log. This results in `'Oh an error: Hello world!'`.
patternExplanation: Tests knowledge of JavaScript scoping, hoisting, and runtime behavior.

title: JS MCQ #6.3: What's the output?
explanation:
When a constructor function is called with the `new` keyword, it creates an object and sets the `this` keyword to refer to that object. By default, if the constructor function doesn't explicitly return anything, it will return the newly created object.

In this case, the constructor function `Car` explicitly returns a new object with `make` set to `"Maserati"`, which overrides the default behavior. Therefore, when `new Car()` is called, the _returned_ object is assigned to `myCar`, resulting in the output being `"Maserati"` when `myCar.make` is accessed.
patternExplanation: Tests knowledge of JavaScript scoping, hoisting, and runtime behavior.

title: JS MCQ #6.4: What's the output?
explanation:
`let x = (y = 10);` is actually shorthand for:

```javascript
y = 10;
let x = y;
```

When we set `y` equal to `10`, we actually add a property `y` to the global object (`window` in the browser, `global` in Node). In a browser, `window.y` is now equal to `10`.

Then, we declare a variable `x` with the value of `y`, which is `10`. Variables declared with the `let` keyword are _block scoped_, they are only defined within the block they're declared in; the immediately invoked function expression (IIFE) in this case. When we use the `typeof` operator, the operand `x` is not defined: we are trying to access `x` outside of the block it's declared in. This means that `x` is not defined. Values who haven't been assigned a value or declared are of type `"undefined"`. `console.log(typeof x)` returns `"undefined"`.

However, we created a global variable `y` when setting `y` equal to `10`. This value is accessible anywhere in our code. `y` is defined, and holds a value of type `"number"`. `console.log(typeof y)` returns `"number"`.

title: JS MCQ #7.1: What's the output?

The `Object.keys` method returns all _enumerable_ property names from an object, in this case only `"name"`.

title: JS MCQ #7.2: What's the output?

The second argument of `JSON.stringify` is the _replacer_. The replacer can either be a function or an array, and lets you control what and how the values should be stringified.

If the replacer is an _array_, only the property names included in the array will be added to the JSON string. In this case, only the properties with the names `"level"` and `"health"` are included, `"username"` is excluded. `data` is now equal to `"{"level":19, "health":90}"`.

If the replacer is a _function_, this function gets called on every property in the object you're stringifying. The value returned from this function will be the value of the property when it's added to the JSON string. If the value is `undefined`, this property is excluded from the JSON string.

title: JS MCQ #7.4: What's the output?
explanation:

The value of the parameter will be the default value, if no other value has been passed to the function, or if the value of the parameter is `"undefined"`. In this case, we spread the properties of the `value` object into a new object, so `x` has the default value of `{ number: 10 }`.

The default argument is evaluated at _call time_! Every time we call the function, a _new_ object is created. We invoke the `multiply` function the first two times without passing a value: `x` has the default value of `{ number: 10 }`. We then log the multiplied value of that number, which is `20`.

The third time we invoke multiply, we do pass an argument: the object called `value`. The `*=` operator is actually shorthand for `x.number = x.number * 2`: we modify the value of `x.number`, and log the multiplied value `20`.

title: JS MCQ #7.5: What's the output?
description:

explanation:
The first argument that the `reduce` method receives is the _accumulator_, `x` in this case. The second argument is the _current value_, `y`. With the reduce method, we execute a callback function on every element in the array, which could ultimately result in one single value.

In this example, we are not returning any values, we are simply logging the values of the accumulator and the current value.

The value of the accumulator is equal to the previously returned value of the callback function. If you don't pass the optional `initialValue` argument to the `reduce` method, the accumulator is equal to the first element on the first call.

On the first call, the accumulator (`x`) is `1`, and the current value (`y`) is `2`. We don't return from the callback function, we log the accumulator, and the current values: `1` and `2` get logged.

If you don't return a value from a function, it returns `undefined`. On the next call, the accumulator is `undefined`, and the current value is `3`. `undefined` and `3` get logged.

On the fourth call, we again don't return from the callback function. The accumulator is again `undefined`, and the current value is `4`. `undefined` and `4` get logged.
patternExplanation: Tests knowledge of JavaScript scoping, hoisting, and runtime behavior.

title: JS MCQ #8.1: How can we log the values that are commented out after the console.log statement?

When we call `game.next("Yes").value`, the previous `yield` is replaced with the value of the parameters passed to the `next()` function, `"Yes"` in this case. title: JS MCQ #8.7: Is this a pure function?
explanation:
A pure function is a function that _always_ returns the same result, if the same arguments are passed.

The `sum` function always returns the same result. If we pass `1` and `2`, it will _always_ return `3` without side effects. If we pass `5` and `10`, it will _always_ return `15`, and so on. This is the definition of a pure function.

title: JS MCQ #8.8: What is the output?
explanation:
The `add` function is a _memoized_ function. With memoization, we can cache the results of a function in order to speed up its execution. In this case, we create a `cache` object that stores the previously returned values.

If we call the `addFunction` function again with the same argument, it first checks whether it has already gotten that value in its cache. If that's the case, the cache value will be returned, which saves execution time. Otherwise, if it's not cached, it will calculate the value and store it afterward.

We call the `addFunction` function three times with the same value: on the first invocation, the value of the function when `num` is equal to `10` isn't cached yet. The condition of the if-statement `num in cache` returns `false`, and the else block gets executed: `Calculated! 20` gets logged, and the value of the result gets added to the cache object. `cache` now looks like `{ 10: 20 }`.

The second time, the `cache` object contains the value that gets returned for `10`. The condition of the if-statement `num in cache` returns `true`, and `'From cache! 20'` gets logged.

The third time, we pass `5 * 2` to the function which gets evaluated to `10`. The `cache` object contains the value that gets returned for `10`. The condition of the if-statement `num in cache` returns `true`, and `'From cache! 20'` gets logged.

We declared the `setTimeout` function on the _global object_, so within the `setTimeout` function, the `this` keyword refers to the _global object_. title: JS MCQ #10.5: What's the output?
explanation:
In JavaScript, we don't _have_ to write the semicolon (`;`) explicitly, however the JavaScript engine still adds them after statements. This is called **Automatic Semicolon Insertion**. A statement can for example be variables, or keywords like `throw`, `return`, `break`, etc.

Here, we wrote a `return` statement, and another value `a + b` on a _new line_. However, since it's a new line, the engine doesn't know that it's actually the value that we wanted to return. Instead, it automatically added a semicolon after `return`. You could see this as:

```javascript
return;
a + b;
```

This means that `a + b` is never reached, since a function stops running after the `return` keyword. If no value gets returned, like here, the function returns `undefined`. Note that there is no automatic insertion after `if/else` statements!

title: JS MCQ #10.7: What's the output?

This is one of the many qualities of a symbol: besides representing an entirely unique value (which prevents accidental name collision on objects, for example when working with 2 libraries that want to add properties to the same object), you can also "hide" properties on objects this way (although not entirely. title: JS MCQ #10.8: What's the output?
description:
What is the output?

```javascript
const getList = ([x, ...y]) => [x, y]
const getUser = user => { name: user.name, age: user.age }

const list = [1, 2, 3, 4]
const user = { name: "Lydia", age: 21 }

console.log(getList(list))
console.log(getUser(user))
```
explanation:
The `getList` function receives an array as its argument. Between the parentheses of the `getList` function, we destructure this array right away. You could see this as:

`[x, ...y] = [1, 2, 3, 4]`

With the rest parameter `...y`, we put all "remaining" arguments in an array. The remaining arguments are `2`, `3` and `4` in this case. The value of `y` is an array, containing all the rest parameters. The value of `x` is equal to `1` in this case, so when we log `[x, y]`, `[1, [2, 3, 4]]` gets logged.

The `getUser` function receives an object. With arrow functions, we don't _have_ to write curly brackets if we just return one value. However, if you want to instantly return an _object_ from an arrow function, you have to write it between parentheses, otherwise everything between the two braces will be interpreted as a block statement. In this case the code between the braces is not a valid JavaScript code, so a `SyntaxError` gets thrown. 

The following function would have returned an object:

`const getUser = user => ({ name: user.name, age: user.age })`

title: JS MCQ #10.9: What's the output?

SyntaxErrors get thrown when you've written something that isn't valid JavaScript, for example when you've written the word `return` as `retrun`.
ReferenceErrors get thrown when JavaScript isn't able to find a reference to a value that you're trying to access.

title: JS MCQ #11.2: What's the value of output?
explanation:
With a promise, we basically say _I want to execute this function, but I'll put it aside for now while it's running since this might take a while. Only when a certain value is resolved (or rejected), and when the call stack is empty, I want to use this value._

We can get this value with both `.then` and the `await` keywords in an `async` function. Although we can get a promise's value with both `.then` and `await`, they work a bit differently.

In the `firstFunction`, we (sort of) put the myPromise function aside while it was running, but continued running the other code, which is `console.log('second')` in this case. Then, the function resolved with the string `I have resolved`, which then got logged after it saw that the callstack was empty.

With the await keyword in `secondFunction`, we literally pause the execution of an async function until the value has been resolved before moving to the next line.

This means that it waited for the `myPromise` to resolve with the value `I have resolved`, and only once that happened, we moved to the next line: `second` got logged.

title: JS MCQ #11.3: What's the value of output?
explanation:
The `+` operator is not only used for adding numerical values, but we can also use it to concatenate strings. Whenever the JavaScript engine sees that one or more values are not a number, it coerces the number into a string.

The first one is `1`, which is a numerical value. `1 + 2` returns the number 3.

However, the second one is a string `"Lydia"`. `"Lydia"` is a string and `2` is a number: `2` gets coerced into a string. `"Lydia"` and `"2"` get concatenated, which results in the string `"Lydia2"`.

`{ name: "Lydia" }` is an object. Neither a number nor an object is a string, so it stringifies both. Whenever we stringify a regular object, it becomes `"[object Object]"`. `"[object Object]"` concatenated with `"2"` becomes `"[object Object]2"`.

If you pass a regular function, it'll be a resolved promise with a regular value. If you pass a promise, it'll be a resolved promise with the resolved value of that passed promise.

In this case, we just passed the numerical value `5`. It returns a resolved promise with the value `5`.

title: JS MCQ #11.5: What's its value?

We set the default value for `person2` equal to the `person` object, and passed the `person` object as the value for `person1`.

title: JS MCQ #11.6: What's its value?
explanation:
In JavaScript, we have two ways to access properties on an object: bracket notation, or dot notation. In this example, we use dot notation (`colorConfig.colors`) instead of bracket notation (`colorConfig["colors"]`).

With dot notation, JavaScript tries to find the property on the object with that exact name. In this example, JavaScript tries to find a property called `colors` on the `colorConfig` object. There is no property called `colors`, so this returns `undefined`. Then, we try to access the value of the first element by using `[1]`. We cannot do this on a value that's `undefined`, so it throws a `TypeError`: `Cannot read property '1' of undefined`.

JavaScript interprets (or unboxes) statements. When we use bracket notation, it sees the first opening bracket `[` and keeps going until it finds the closing bracket `]`. Only then, it will evaluate the statement. If we would've used `colorConfig[colors[1]]`, it would have returned the value of the `red` property on the `colorConfig` object.

title: JS MCQ #11.9: What's the output?
explanation:
We set the value of the `favoriteFood` property on the `info` object equal to the string with the pizza emoji, `'🍕'`. A string is a primitive data type. In JavaScript, primitive data types don't interact by reference.

In JavaScript, primitive data types (everything that's not an object) interact by _value_. In this case, we set the value of the `favoriteFood` property on the `info` object equal to the value of the first element in the `food` array, the string with the pizza emoji in this case (`'🍕'`). A string is a primitive data type, and interact by value (see my [blogpost](https://www.theavocoder.com/complete-javascript/2018/12/21/by-value-vs-by-reference) if you're interested in learning more)

Then, we change the value of the `favoriteFood` property on the `info` object. The `food` array hasn't changed, since the value of `favoriteFood` was merely a _copy_ of the value of the first element in the array, and doesn't have a reference to the same spot in memory as the element on `food[0]`. When we log food, it's still the original array, `['🍕', '🍫', '🥑', '🍔']`.

title: JS MCQ #12.2: What's the output?
explanation:
With the `yield` keyword, we `yield` values in a generator function. With the `yield*` keyword, we can yield values from another generator function, or iterable object (for example an array).

In `generatorOne`, we yield the entire array `['a', 'b', 'c']` using the `yield` keyword. The value of `value` property on the object returned by the `next` method on `one` (`one.next().value`) is equal to the entire array `['a', 'b', 'c']`.

```javascript
console.log(one.next().value); // ['a', 'b', 'c']
console.log(one.next().value); // undefined
```

In `generatorTwo`, we use the `yield*` keyword. This means that the first yielded value of `two`, is equal to the first yielded value in the iterator. The iterator is the array `['a', 'b', 'c']`. The first yielded value is `a`, so the first time we call `two.next().value`, `a` is returned.

```javascript
console.log(two.next().value); // 'a'
console.log(two.next().value); // 'b'
console.log(two.next().value); // 'c'
console.log(two.next().value); // undefined
```

title: JS MCQ #12.4: What will happen?
options: The `setInterval` callback will still be called every second
explanation:
Normally when we set objects equal to `null`, those objects get _garbage collected_ as there is no reference anymore to that object. However, since the callback function within `setInterval` is an arrow function (thus bound to the `config` object), the callback function still holds a reference to the `config` object. 
As long as there is a reference, the object won't get garbage collected. 
Since this is an interval, setting `config` to `null` or `delete`-ing `config.alert` won't garbage-collect the interval, so the interval will still be called. 
It should be cleared with `clearInterval(config.alert)` to remove it from memory.
Since it was not cleared, the `setInterval` callback function will still get invoked every 1000ms (1s).

title: JS MCQ #14.3: What's the output?
options: `Promise 1! Last line 1! Promise 2! Last line 2! Timeout 1! Timeout 2!`
`Last line 1! Timeout 1! Promise 1! Last line 2! Promise2! Timeout 2! `
`Last line 1! Promise 2! Last line 2! Promise 1! Timeout 1! Timeout 2!`
`Timeout 1! Promise 1! Last line 1! Promise 2! Timeout 2! Last line 2!`
explanation: First, we invoke `funcOne`. On the first line of `funcOne`, we call the _asynchronous_ `setTimeout` function, from which the callback is sent to the Web API. (see my article on the event loop here.) Then we call the `myPromise` promise, which is an _asynchronous_ operation. Pay attention, that now only the first then clause was added to the microtask queue. Both the promise and the timeout are asynchronous operations, the function keeps on running while it's busy completing the promise and handling the `setTimeout` callback. This means that `Last line 1!` gets logged first, since this is not an asynchonous operation. Since the callstack is not empty yet, the `setTimeout` function and promise in `funcOne` cannot get added to the callstack yet. In `funcTwo`, the variable `res` gets `Promise` because `Promise.resolve(Promise.resolve('Promise'))` is equivalent to `Promise.resolve('Promise')` since resolving a promise just resolves it's value. The `await` in this line stops the execution of the function until it receives the resolution of the promise and then keeps on running synchronously until completion, so `Promise 2!` and then `Last line 2!` are logged and the `setTimeout` is sent to the Web API. If the first then clause in `funcOne` had its own log statement, it would be printed before `Promise 2!`. Howewer, it executed silently and put the second then clause in microtask queue. So, the second clause will be printed after `Promise 2!`. Then the call stack is empty. Promises are _microtasks_ so they are resolved first when the call stack is empty so `Promise 1!` gets to be logged. Now, since `funcTwo` popped off the call stack, the call stack is empty. The callbacks waiting in the queue (`() => console.log("Timeout 1!")` from `funcOne`, and `() => console.log("Timeout 2!")` from `funcTwo`) get added to the call stack one by one. The first callback logs `Timeout 1!`, and gets popped off the stack. Then, the second callback logs `Timeout 2!`, and gets popped off the stack.

description:

title: JS Theory: V8 Hidden Classes & Property Insertion Order
options: Both functions create objects with identical hidden classes because their final properties have the same names and types.
They produce objects with different hidden classes because property addition order dictates the shape transition tree.
V8 automatically sorts object keys alphabetically during compilation to merge equivalent shapes.
Hidden classes are only allocated when using the class keyword with constructor.
explanation: In V8 and JavaScriptCore, objects begin with an empty hidden class. Adding properties transitions the object along a shape tree: createPointA follows empty -> shape(x) -> shape(x, y), whereas createPointB follows empty -> shape(y) -> shape(y, x). Because property offsets and transition paths differ, they have different hidden classes. Mixing both at a single function callsite causes inline caches to deoptimize.
patternExplanation: Always initialize object fields in the same order (or initialize in constructors) to allow V8 to reuse shapes and monomorphic inline caches.

title: JS Theory: Monomorphic vs Megamorphic Inline Caches
description: In modern JavaScript engines (V8, SpiderMonkey), what is the difference between a Monomorphic and a Megamorphic Inline Cache (IC) when accessing a property `obj.foo`?
options: A monomorphic IC has seen only 1 object shape and generates direct memory offset loads; a megamorphic IC has seen 5+ shapes and falls back to a global hash table lookup.
Monomorphic ICs work only with primitive values, while megamorphic ICs handle object references.
Monomorphic ICs store data on the call stack, while megamorphic ICs allocate cache entries on the heap.
Megamorphic ICs are faster than monomorphic ICs because they utilize multi-threaded speculative execution.
explanation: Inline Caches (ICs) record observed object shapes at property access sites. If a site only ever encounters 1 shape, it is Monomorphic, allowing compiled code to load the property directly from a fixed memory offset. If it encounters 2-4 shapes, it is Polymorphic. If it encounters 5 or more shapes, it becomes Megamorphic and falls back to generic hash table lookup, significantly degrading throughput.
patternExplanation: Avoid passing objects with differing shapes into hot loops and utility functions to prevent inline caches from becoming megamorphic.

title: JS Theory: Event Loop Execution Order & Microtasks
explanation: 1 and 6 log synchronously. Next, the microtask queue runs: the first Promise callback logs 3 and enqueues queueMicrotask(4). Then .then(5) is queued after the first Promise resolves. The microtask queue processes sequentially: 4 is at the front of the microtask queue followed by 5. Finally, the microtask queue empties, and the macrotask setTimeout callback runs, logging 2.
patternExplanation: Microtasks (Promise reactions, queueMicrotask) run continuously until the microtask queue is completely empty before the browser yields to rendering or macrotasks.

title: JS Theory: Generational Garbage Collection in V8
description: How does V8 divide memory in its Generational Garbage Collector to minimize pause times?
options: Memory is partitioned into a Young Generation (nursery semi-spaces) collected frequently with Cheney's copying algorithm (Scavenger), and an Old Generation collected with Mark-Sweep-Compact.
Memory is divided into Stack memory for numbers and booleans, and Heap memory for arrays and objects, with GC only running on the Stack.
V8 relies exclusively on reference counting; cyclic references are resolved through a secondary thread without pauses.
Memory is dynamically allocated in 64MB chunks and freed immediately when functions return, eliminating the need for GC cycles.
explanation: V8 is based on the Weak Generational Hypothesis: most objects die young. It divides the heap into the Young Generation (Semi-spaces: From-Space and To-Space), collected rapidly by the Scavenger algorithm. Objects that survive multiple scavenges are tenured into the Old Generation, which is garbage collected less frequently using incremental Mark-Sweep-Compact.
patternExplanation: Understanding generational GC helps explain why allocating temporary objects inside tight loops triggers frequent minor GC scavenges.

title: JS Theory: WeakRef and FinalizationRegistry
description: What is the primary characteristic of ECMAScript `WeakRef` and `FinalizationRegistry`?
options: WeakRef prevents garbage collection until deref() is called, whereas FinalizationRegistry forces immediate synchronous memory deallocation.
WeakRef allows holding a reference to an object without preventing it from being garbage-collected, and FinalizationRegistry requests a callback after the target object is reclaimed.
WeakRef converts any object into a primitive symbol that persists across browser reloads.
FinalizationRegistry guarantees that its cleanup callback will execute synchronously in the same tick the object is dereferenced.
explanation: WeakRef holds a weak reference to a target object, returning the object via weakRef.deref() if it is still alive or undefined if collected. FinalizationRegistry allows registering a cleanup callback that will be called after the object has been garbage collected. Note that the timing of garbage collection and registry callbacks is non-deterministic.
patternExplanation: WeakRef is useful for memory-sensitive caches, but applications must not rely on exact GC timing or cleanup callback execution.

title: JS Theory: Proxy Traps and Invariant Enforcement
options: It returns 999 because the Proxy handler intercepts all property accesses.
It returns 42 because proxies automatically bypass non-configurable properties.
It throws a TypeError because Proxy handlers are strictly prohibited from violating target invariants.
It returns undefined because conflicting property descriptors are silenced.
explanation: The ECMAScript specification enforces 'invariants' on Proxy handlers to preserve core language integrity. If target property is non-configurable and non-writable, the get trap MUST return the exact same value as the target property. Returning any other value throws a TypeError: 'get' on proxy: property is read-only and non-configurable on target, but the proxy did not return its actual value.
patternExplanation: Proxy traps cannot contradict the invariants of non-configurable or non-extensible target properties.

title: JS Theory: Symbol.toPrimitive Coercion Algorithm
description: What hints does the `Symbol.toPrimitive` method receive during type conversion?
explanation: The well-known symbol Symbol.toPrimitive specifies a method called to convert an object to a corresponding primitive value. It is invoked with one of three string hints: 'number' (e.g. unary +, Math methods), 'string' (e.g. String(), template literals), or 'default' (e.g. binary +, loose equality == where both number and string are permissible).
patternExplanation: Symbol.toPrimitive takes precedence over valueOf() and toString() when converting objects to primitives.

title: JS Theory: ESM Live Bindings vs CommonJS Value Copies
description: How do ES Module (ESM) exports differ fundamentally from CommonJS module.exports when an exported variable is mutated inside the exporting module?
options: ESM exports are 'live bindings' (read-only views of the exporter internal variables), reflecting updates when mutated; CommonJS exports copy values onto an exported object at the time of execution.
CommonJS supports live bindings via getters, while ESM creates static immutable snapshots that never change.
ESM clones all exported values using structured cloning upon import to ensure thread safety.
Both module systems behave identically because JavaScript runs in a single-threaded event loop.
explanation: In ESM, export let count = 0 creates a live binding. When count++ executes in the exporting module, any importing module reading count observes the updated value in real-time. In CommonJS, module.exports = { count } evaluates once and copies the primitive value; subsequent mutations in the exporting file do not alter the imported object property.
patternExplanation: ESM modules create live bindings that reflect runtime updates, unlike CommonJS module exports which capture values at load time.

title: JS Theory: Scope Sharing and Closure Memory Leaks
options: Both unused and someMethod share the same lexical scope environment record; because theThing.someMethod is retained, the entire scope (including originalThing) remains retained in memory.
setInterval retains a strong reference to the entire global object on each tick.
new Array().join() cannot be collected by V8 garbage collectors.
Arrow functions are required in intervals to release inner scope closures.
explanation: This is the classic Meteor closure memory leak. In V8, functions created within the same lexical context share the same scope object. Because someMethod is retained on theThing, its parent scope remains alive. That scope contains originalThing, which points to the previous theThing, creating an uncollectable linked chain of large arrays on every interval invocation.
patternExplanation: Closures in the same lexical block share a scope environment. If one closure is retained, unreferenced variables captured by sibling closures can be kept alive in memory.

title: JS Theory: Layout Thrashing (Forced Synchronous Layout)
description: What causes 'Layout Thrashing' in web applications, and how should it be avoided?
options: Alternating between writing to the DOM (e.g. el.style.width) and reading geometric properties (e.g. el.offsetWidth) in a loop, forcing the browser to recalculate layout repeatedly.
Using CSS grid instead of flexbox for complex responsive layouts.
Attaching multiple click event listeners to child elements instead of using event delegation.
Rendering canvas elements alongside SVG graphics on the main thread.
explanation: Browsers batch style and layout calculations lazily. However, when code modifies an element style and immediately asks for geometric information (e.g. offsetWidth, clientHeight, getBoundingClientRect), the browser is forced to flush pending style changes and perform a synchronous layout. Doing this in a loop causes repeated forced reflows, known as Layout Thrashing. To prevent it, batch all reads first, then batch all writes.
patternExplanation: Always batch DOM layout reads before DOM writes, or use requestAnimationFrame to schedule writes on the next frame.

title: JS Theory: GPU Compositing Layers & will-change
description: What is the benefit and potential downside of promoting an element to its own GPU Compositing Layer using `will-change: transform`?
options: Benefit: Transformations can be animated on the compositor thread without triggering layout or paint; Downside: Excessive layers consume significant GPU VRAM and can cause memory exhaustion.
Benefit: The element executes JavaScript on a background web worker thread; Downside: CSS animations are disabled.
Benefit: The element becomes immune to XSS attacks; Downside: It cannot receive pointer events.
Benefit: Reduces network latency for image assets; Downside: Degrades SEO ranking.
explanation: Promoting an element to a composite layer allows the compositor thread on the GPU to handle transforms and opacity changes directly, bypassing both layout and paint on the CPU main thread. However, each layer requires its own bitmap stored in GPU memory. Creating too many layers consumes vast amounts of VRAM and CPU-GPU bandwidth.
patternExplanation: Use will-change sparingly and remove it when animations finish to prevent unnecessary GPU memory consumption.

title: JS Theory: SameSite Cookie Attributes & CSRF
description: How does `SameSite=Lax` cookie behavior protect users against Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF)?
options: Cookies are withheld on cross-site requests (like POST forms or image embeds), but are sent when the user navigates top-level to the origin site (e.g. following a standard link).
Cookies are never sent under any cross-origin circumstances, even when clicking an external link.
Cookies are encrypted using the client public key before transmission.
Cookies can only be accessed by JavaScript running inside HTTPS iframes.
explanation: SameSite=Lax blocks cookies from being sent on cross-site subrequests (such as cross-origin POST forms, AJAX fetch requests, or images), preventing classic CSRF exploits. However, it still attaches cookies on safe top-level navigations (e.g. clicking a standard GET link to the site from an external search engine).
patternExplanation: SameSite=Lax is the modern browser default and provides baseline CSRF defense for state-changing cross-origin requests.

title: JS Theory: Asynchronous Generators & Backpressure
description: How does the `for await...of` loop handle backpressure when consuming an asynchronous generator?
options: It pauses consumption and does not invoke .next() on the generator until the promise returned by the current iteration has fulfilled.
It reads all generator yields concurrently and buffers them in an internal FIFO queue.
It drops items if the consumer takes longer than 16.6ms to process each item.
It spawns a background Web Worker to consume the generator in parallel.
explanation: for await...of guarantees sequential processing. It awaits the promise returned by iterator.next(), executes the loop body with the resolved value, and only requests the next item after the current loop iteration completes. This naturally provides backpressure, preventing fast producers from overwhelming slow consumers.
patternExplanation: for await...of provides built-in backpressure by waiting for both the yield promise and loop body execution before pulling the next value.

title: JS Theory: Object.create(null) vs Object Literal {}
description: Why is `Object.create(null)` preferred over `{}` when implementing a pure hash map or key-value lookup table?
options: Object.create(null) has no prototype (__proto__ is undefined), preventing collisions with built-in properties like toString, valueOf, or prototype pollution attacks.
Object.create(null) allocates memory directly in the nursery space without garbage collection.
Object.create(null) is an immutable data structure by default.
Object.create(null) automatically converts string keys into 64-bit integer hashes.
explanation: A standard object literal {} inherits from Object.prototype, containing properties like hasOwnProperty, toString, constructor, and __proto__. If user input supplies a key matching one of these names, it can overwrite methods or manipulate prototype chains. Object.create(null) has a prototype of null, making every key lookup safe.
patternExplanation: Use Object.create(null) or Map for dictionary lookups to eliminate prototype property collisions and prototype pollution vulnerabilities.

title: JS Theory: Structured Clone Algorithm Capabilities
description: Which of the following data types CANNOT be cloned using the native `structuredClone()` API?
explanation: structuredClone() supports circular references, Sets, Maps, Dates, RegExps, TypedArrays, and Error objects. However, attempting to clone Functions, DOM Nodes, or Symbols throws a DataCloneError.
patternExplanation: structuredClone handles complex nested structures and cyclic graphs, but cannot serialize executable functions or DOM elements.

title: JS Theory: Promise.any vs Promise.race Failure Semantics
description: How does `Promise.any()` differ from `Promise.race()` when the first settling promise rejects?
options: Promise.race() rejects immediately with the first rejection reason; Promise.any() ignores rejections and waits for the first fulfillment, only rejecting with an AggregateError if all promises reject.
Promise.any() returns the first rejected promise, while Promise.race() returns null.
Promise.any() catches synchronous errors, while Promise.race() throws unhandled rejections.
Both methods reject immediately if any promise in the array fails.
explanation: Promise.race settles as soon as ANY promise settles (whether fulfilled or rejected). If the fastest promise rejects, Promise.race rejects immediately. Conversely, Promise.any looks for the first FULFILLED promise. It ignores individual rejections until ALL promises reject, in which case it rejects with an AggregateError containing all errors.
patternExplanation: Use Promise.any when you need the fastest successful response (e.g. querying fallback mirrors), and Promise.race when timeout or earliest cancellation is needed.

title: JS Theory: DOM Event Propagation & Delegation
description: What are the three sequential phases of DOM event dispatch as defined by the W3C Event specification?
options: Capture Phase (Root down to target) -> Target Phase -> Bubble Phase (Target up to root)
Bubble Phase -> Target Phase -> Capture Phase
Trigger Phase -> Propagation Phase -> Resolution Phase
Dispatch Phase -> Listener Phase -> GC Phase
explanation: When an event occurs, it first travels down the DOM tree from the window and document to the target during the Capture Phase. Next, it triggers listeners registered directly on the target during the Target Phase. Finally, it bubbles back up through ancestor elements to the root during the Bubble Phase (unless event.stopPropagation() is called).
patternExplanation: addEventListener(type, handler, true) registers for the capture phase, whereas addEventListener(type, handler, false) registers for the bubble phase.

title: JS Theory: Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ) Mechanics
options: Parameter default values evaluate in an intermediate scope where parameter `x` is already hoisted but in its Temporal Dead Zone prior to parameter assignment.
Default parameters cannot reference any variables outside the function.
The variable `x` is private to the module and cannot be read as a default argument.
Function arguments can only be primitives, not identifiers.
explanation: Function parameters form their own scope during invocation. In `function test(y = x, x)`, the parameter identifier `x` shadows the outer `let x = 10`. When `y = x` evaluates, parameter `x` is in its Temporal Dead Zone (declared in parameter scope but not yet initialized), throwing a ReferenceError: Cannot access x before initialization.
patternExplanation: Parameter default expressions evaluate from left to right in their own scope. An earlier parameter cannot reference a later parameter because the later parameter is in TDZ.

title: JS Theory: React Concurrent Mode & Fiber Reentrancy
description: In React 18+ Concurrent Mode, how does the Fiber architecture enable time-slicing and interruptible rendering?
options: The component tree is represented as a linked-list of Fiber nodes; the work loop checks `shouldYield()` between fibers and can yield control to the browser main thread to process user input before resuming.
React compiles all components into WebAssembly threads that execute concurrently on separate CPU cores.
Virtual DOM elements are rendered directly onto a hidden OffscreenCanvas using WebGL.
React overrides the browser V8 garbage collector to prevent pauses during state updates.
explanation: Unlike the old recursive stack reconciler which blocked the main thread until the entire tree rendered, Fiber models the tree as a linked list (child, sibling, return pointers). The work loop processes units of work one fiber at a time. After processing a fiber, it checks if the 5ms deadline has passed via the Scheduler. If so, it pauses, yields to the browser for user input or frame rendering, and later resumes.
patternExplanation: Fiber enables interruptible rendering by breaking component tree reconciliation into cooperative units of work along a linked list.

title: JS Theory: Interaction to Next Paint (INP) vs First Input Delay (FID)
description: Why did Google replace First Input Delay (FID) with Interaction to Next Paint (INP) as a Core Web Vital?
options: FID only measured the input delay of the very first user interaction; INP measures the worst-case interaction latency (input delay + processing time + presentation delay) across the entire page lifecycle.
FID was incompatible with mobile devices, whereas INP only measures touch events.
INP measures network round-trip time, while FID measured CPU temperature.
FID required server-side tracking, while INP is computed in the Service Worker.
explanation: First Input Delay (FID) only captured the time between the user first interaction (e.g. click) and when the main thread began processing the event handler. It ignored the time taken to run the event handler and the time for the browser to paint the visual update. INP addresses this by measuring the end-to-end responsiveness of all interactions throughout the page visit.
patternExplanation: Optimizing INP requires breaking up long JavaScript tasks and yielding to the main thread with setTimeout or scheduler.yield() before updating UI.
